Description: An Egyptian wisdom text of thirty short chapters, a father's advice to his son, preserved on Papyrus British Museum EA 10474, bought by the British Museum in 1888 and said to come from el-Hiba. Most likely composed between about 1300 and 1000 BC, it was published in 1923, and in 1924 Adolf Erman showed that Proverbs 22:17-24:22 runs closely alongside it: both open with 'incline your ear' and 'apply your heart,' both warn against moving the ancient boundary stone, and both picture ill-gotten wealth sprouting wings and flying away.
Interpretations: The parallels are real and close, and most scholars think the direction ran from Egypt to Israel through scribal training, with the Hebrew writer adapting rather than copying: Proverbs grounds the same maxims in the fear of Yahweh ('for the LORD will plead their case,' Proverbs 22:23) rather than in Egyptian ma'at. The thirty chapters of Amenemope also help explain the 'thirty sayings' of Proverbs 22:20. This is a parallel that illuminates how biblical wisdom literature was composed, not a challenge to inspiration: Scripture itself presents Proverbs as gathered wisdom.
AlternativeNames: Instruction of Amenemope; Papyrus BM EA 10474
BiblicalSignificance: It is the closest known parallel to a whole section of Proverbs, showing that Israel's sages worked within a wider ancient Near Eastern wisdom tradition while reshaping it around the fear of the LORD.
ArtifactDate: Composed c. 1300-1000 BC; papyrus late New Kingdom
